naive_1to1_mapping_safety_assessment.explanation: Safety of a naive numeric 1:1 mapping depends entirely on the specific country pair and cannot be assumed uniformly. It is reasonably safe for US<->Turkiye (both use ascending 9-12 numbering with functionally equivalent school-starting-age conventions, so grade N carries the same age range in both systems for an on-time student). It is UNSAFE for US<->UK: UK Year numbering is offset by one full year relative to US grade numbering because English year groups count from an earlier anchor point (Year 1 begins the September a child turns 5-6) than US grades do, so UK Year N is age-equivalent to US Grade (N-1), not Grade N. It BREAKS DOWN STRUCTURALLY (not just by an offset) for France, where the last four years of secondary schooling straddle two different institution types (collège and lycée) with non-numeric, descending-order names (Troisième/Seconde/Première/Terminale) that cannot be parsed as numbers at all. It is AMBIGUOUS for Germany, where the same nominal grade label ('Klasse 12') denotes the final pre-university year in G8 states but the second-to-last year in G9 states -- the correct interpretation depends on which Bundesland/track the school follows, information a naive numeric mapping does not capture. It is NOT APPLICABLE for the IB Diploma Programme, whose own official eligibility framing (per IBO) is age-based (16-19) rather than grade-number-based; the programme's two years are labeled using whatever host-country numbering the school already has, so 'IB DP1' alone carries no inherent grade number to map.

Correspondingly: UK Year 10 <-> US Grade 9 (age 14-15), Year 11 <-> Grade 10 (age 15-16), Year 12 <-> Grade 11 (age 16-17), Year 13 <-> Grade 12 (age 17-18).

proposed_normalization_approach.description: ORYN should not store or match on raw grade-number strings across countries. Instead, define a canonical, AGE-anchored 'secondary_stage' enum (S1-S4) for the last four years of pre-tertiary schooling, where each stage is defined primarily by its typical age range, with a per-country lookup table translating each country's own grade/year label into the corresponding canonical stage. Eligibility matching for a given opportunity should run on whichever of (a) explicit age range or (b) canonical stage the opportunity itself states, converting the ORYN user's country-specific grade label into both an age estimate and a canonical stage at profile-entry time (using the country's own on-time-progression convention), rather than ever comparing raw grade-number strings across two different countries directly. Countries whose terminology doesn't reduce to a clean number (France) or whose grade number is ambiguous without extra context (Germany's G8/G9) get an explicit country-specific resolver rather than being forced into the same lookup shape as US/UK/Turkey.

cases_that_dont_map_cleanly: Germany G9 states (e.g. Bavaria) have a 5th year (Klasse 13) beyond canonical S4 that is the actual final/Abitur year -- a 'S4 = final year' assumption is wrong for roughly half of German states; ORYN needs a per-Bundesland G8/G9 flag, not just a country flag, to place a German student correctly.

France's S1-equivalent year (age 14-15, Troisième) is institutionally part of collège, not lycée -- so a French student's 'first of the last 4 secondary years' is enrolled in a different school type than their Seconde/Première/Terminale years; any UI or matching logic that assumes 'last 4 years of secondary = one continuous high school' will misrepresent the French case.

IB DP does not have its own grade-number system at all -- IBO's authoritative eligibility criterion is age (16-19), and 'DP1/DP2' is descriptive shorthand riding on top of whatever host-country numbering (Year 12/13, Grade 11/12, Klasse 12/13, etc.) the school already uses. ORYN should treat 'IB DP' as a curriculum tag layered on top of a student's host-country grade, not as an independent grade system to map.

Individual students who repeated a year, skipped a year, or enrolled early/late will have a grade label that does not match the typical age for their canonical stage in any country -- the mapping table gives the ON-TIME/modal correspondence only, and should never be used to override a student's or a program's own directly-stated age or grade criterion when both are available.

patterns_found: Both required independently (AND gate): several selective, single-institution research/academic programs (Simons, RSI, Telluride/TASS, Genius Olympiad) state a grade requirement AND a separately-defined age requirement that a student must satisfy simultaneously; nothing in their materials treats one as derivable from the other.

Grade stated as the sole authoritative gate; age mentioned only descriptively/inconsistently: Yale Young Global Scholars codifies eligibility in grade terms ('Grade 10 or 11 ... at the time of application') while separate program materials describe the age range differently in different places (15-17 vs 16-18) -- illustrating that descriptive age text should never be parsed as a strict filter when a grade-based rule is the actual codified gate.

Grade/year as primary gate, age as a soft ceiling with a documented, named exception for non-traditional-age students: Sutton Trust ties eligibility to UK Year group but layers a 'generally under 18' expectation on top, and explicitly documents that some partner universities waive that ceiling for over-18 students still in the qualifying year group -- i.e. the program itself resolves the grade/age tension for atypical students rather than leaving it to inference.

Age partially decouples from eligibility itself and instead modifies a different requirement: Genius Olympiad's age-13 floor is a hard eligibility gate, but its age-18 threshold changes only whether an adult chaperone is required, not admission eligibility -- age criteria are not always a binary eligible/ineligible signal.

Grade-only criteria resolve mixed-grade/age group entries via the grade axis alone: National History Day, which states no age criterion at all, resolves group projects spanning multiple grades by placing the whole group in the division (Junior 6-8 / Senior 9-12) of its oldest member -- a real, sourced example of a grade-based (not age-based) tie-break rule for a scenario ORYN's task description flagged (mixed-level participants).

unsafe_inferences: Do not assume UK 'Year N' equals US 'Grade N' for the same number. UK Year 12 (first year of A-Levels/Sixth Form, ages 16-17) is age-equivalent to US Grade 11 (junior year, ages 16-17), not Grade 12. The verified offset is UK Year N <-> US Grade (N-1) across the secondary range (Year 10-13 <-> Grade 9-12).

Do not assume a Turkish '9. sınıf' (or any sınıf number) student's age from the grade number alone without checking whether a program's stated criterion is grade-based or age-based -- even though the on-time Turkey<->US numeric correspondence is safe in the aggregate/typical case, an individual student's actual age can diverge (grade repetition, early/late enrollment, accelerated track), so a directly-stated age (when a program gives one) should always take precedence over an age inferred from the grade label.

Do not assume a German 'Klasse 12' student is in their final pre-university year. In G9 (9-year Gymnasium) states, Klasse 12 is the second-to-last year (final year is Klasse 13); in G8 states, Klasse 12 IS the final year. The correct interpretation requires knowing the state/school's G8-vs-G9 track, not just the country.

Do not parse French 'Seconde', 'Première', or 'Terminale' as if they were numbered grades, and do not assume a US-style 'grade 9-12' 4-year window maps onto a single French institution -- the age-14-15 year (equivalent to US Grade 9 / UK Year 10) is institutionally part of collège (Troisième), not lycée, in the French system.

Do not treat 'IB DP1' or 'IB DP2' as directly convertible to a specific US grade number without knowing the host school's own grade-numbering convention. IBO's own authoritative eligibility criterion for the DP is age-based (16-19), not a DP-specific grade number; 'DP1/DP2' is informal shorthand riding on top of whatever numbering the host country/school already uses.

Do not assume a program's descriptive/illustrative age text (e.g., marketing copy saying participants are 'typically 15-17') is a binding eligibility filter when the program's actual codified rule is grade-based (as seen with Yale Young Global Scholars, where two different official materials give two different descriptive age ranges for the same grade-based rule).

Do not apply one universal 'age as of X date' convention to all opportunities. Real programs measure age as of the program start (Simons), a fixed calendar date unrelated to the program's own start (RSI: July 1), a bounded start/end range (Telluride), or not at all (grade-only programs like National History Day) -- defaulting to a single assumed convention will misclassify eligibility for students near a cutoff.

Do not infer a missing grade or age field for an opportunity by back-calculating from the other field using a typical age-per-grade chart, when the program itself only published one of the two dimensions (e.g., National History Day states grades 6-12 with no age at all; some Economics Olympiad variants state ages 14-18 with no grade at all). Fabricating the missing dimension risks silently excluding or including students the program never actually screened on that axis.

Do not assume grade and age criteria are always jointly required (AND) versus independently sufficient (OR) without checking the specific program's language -- most researched examples that state both treat them as AND (both must be satisfied), but this was not universal or explicitly guaranteed across all programs studied, and no researched example gave explicit guidance for the case where they conflict (see unresolved_questions).
safe_inferences: Within the US, and within Türkiye (given its verified age-aligned convention with the US), typical on-time progression is approximately one grade per age-year, with Grade/sınıf 9 starting around age 14 and Grade/sınıf 12 finishing around age 18 -- usable as a default estimate ONLY when a program does not itself state an age, and clearly labeled as an estimate rather than a program-stated fact.

When a program explicitly states both a grade requirement and an age requirement (e.g., Simons: grade 11 AND age >=16 by program start; RSI: junior year AND age >=16 by July 1), ORYN should store and evaluate both independently as separate, jointly-required gates -- not derive one from the other or treat them as redundant.

When a program states only a grade requirement (no age given, e.g., National History Day), ORYN should leave the age eligibility fields (minimum_age/maximum_age) null/unknown rather than back-filling them from a generic age-per-grade chart -- the absence of an age criterion in the source is itself meaningful information.
When a program states only an age requirement (no grade given, e.g., the Econ Olympiad variant researched here), ORYN should leave eligible_grades null/unknown for the same reason.

A student's self-reported country plus current grade/year label can be safely converted to an approximate age range for matching purposes ONLY when that specific country-pair's offset/structure has been explicitly verified and encoded (Turkiye<->US: safe direct mapping; UK<->US: apply the verified -1 Year-to-Grade offset; France and Germany: apply the documented special-case resolvers) -- never apply one single global numeric-offset constant across all countries.

When both a program's grade criterion and a student's profile grade are available and match, and no age criterion is stated by the program, it is safe to treat the student as grade-eligible without further age verification -- the program has signaled that grade alone is its intended screen.
unresolved_questions: No researched program (Simons, RSI, Telluride, YYGS, Sutton Trust, Genius Olympiad, National History Day) publishes an explicit tie-break rule for the case where a student's grade and age genuinely conflict (e.g., an accelerated student who is Grade 11 but only 15, or a grade-repeating student who is Grade 11 but already 18-19). ORYN cannot assume a universal resolution from the evidence gathered and should likely route such profiles to manual or AI-assisted review rather than auto-determining eligibility either way.

citizenship_vs_residency_vs_school_locat.distinction_explanation: These are three legally and practically distinct tests, and real programs use all three independently: (1) CITIZENSHIP/immigration status -- a passport or green-card fact about the person, unrelated to where they currently live or study (Simons, Davidson Fellows, NASA, RSI's 'citizens and permanent residents' branch); (2) RESIDENCY/domicile -- where the person is legally or physically based, which can be a country or a sub-national unit like a US state (NC Governor's School requires NC residency specifically, not just US citizenship -- a US citizen resident of Georgia is not eligible); (3) CURRENT SCHOOL ENROLLMENT LOCATION -- which school/country the student is physically attending right now, independent of both citizenship and legal residency (MIT PRIMES: 'reside in the United States' / attending a US school -- a Turkish citizen attending a US high school on a student visa qualifies, while a US citizen attending school in Turkey does not). A single program can even combine two of these as alternate qualifying paths (QuestBridge: US high school ENROLLMENT, OR citizenship+PR status if living abroad) or layer a citizenship carve-out on top of a school-location gate (DAAD RISE: university location in US/Canada/UK/Ireland, PLUS a separate exclusion for German citizens unless they've lived outside Germany 6+ years).
citizenship_vs_residency_vs_school_locat.real_example_illustrating_the_difference: A Turkish citizen enrolled at a public high school in North Carolina: ELIGIBLE for MIT PRIMES-USA (school-location test only, citizenship irrelevant) and INELIGIBLE for NC Governor's School (requires NC residency/domicile, and explicitly excludes exchange students even though they may attend an NC school) and INELIGIBLE for Simons Summer Research Program or Davidson Fellows (require actual US citizenship or a green card, and physical school enrollment in the US does not substitute for that status). Three different verdicts for the same student across three real, currently active programs -- proof that citizenship, residency, and school-location are not interchangeable and cannot be safely collapsed into one field.
citizenship_vs_residency_vs_school_locat.gap_assessment_against_orn_current_schem: ORYN's current 3-field model (eligible_countries array + citizenship_restrictions text + residency_restrictions text) has no dedicated field for 'current school enrollment location,' which is a genuinely distinct and commonly-used eligibility axis (MIT PRIMES, QuestBridge's first path, NC Governor's School, Sutton Trust). Today that criterion has nowhere clean to live and would either get force-fit into residency_restrictions (plausible but conflates domicile with school attendance -- these differ for boarding-school and exchange students) or get missed entirely. citizenship_restrictions and residency_restrictions as free text can technically hold any of these facts, but because there is no structured 'restriction_basis' enum (citizenship | permanent_residency | domicile_residency | school_enrollment_location | national_quota_nomination), there is no way to query or display 'is this a citizenship test or a residency test' programmatically, and no way to prevent exactly the kind of multi-fact conflation already visible in ORYN's own Tisch NYU row (age + housing + citizenship/visa-documentation all crammed into residency_restrictions). eligible_countries as a flat array is also structurally unable to represent sub-national restrictions (NC Governor's School is state-level, not country-level) or nomination-mediated eligibility (EUCYS/UWC/ISEF, where 'is this country eligible' is the wrong question -- the right question is 'does this country currently have an active national organiser/affiliate, and did the student win/get nominated there').
citizenship_vs_residency_vs_school_locat.recommended_direction: Add a structured restriction_basis enum per opportunity (citizenship, permanent_residency, domicile_residency, school_enrollment_location, national_quota_nomination, none_stated) alongside the existing free-text fields, and consider a separate school_location_restrictions text field distinct from residency_restrictions so domicile and school-attendance facts are not forced into the same slot.

visa_documentation_vs_eligibility_distin.explanation: Eligibility answers 'are you the kind of applicant this program accepts at all' (a yes/no gate based on citizenship, residency, or school location). Visa/documentation requirements answer a completely different, later-stage question: 'given that you ARE eligible and admitted, what travel/immigration paperwork must you personally arrange to physically attend.' Conflating the two is a real and harmful error for an international student -- telling a Turkish student a program is 'restricted' because it mentions F-1 visas would incorrectly turn them away from a program that actually welcomes them and merely expects them to handle their own visa application, exactly as any international student attending any US program must. The three examples researched show a spectrum: pure logistics disclaimer with zero eligibility implication (Telluride: 'we cannot assist with visas,' eligibility itself unaffected), a factual note about which visa category applies (PROMYS: visitor visa, not F-1 -- purely informational, no eligibility gate), and a procedural requirement that is functionally closer to a soft eligibility gate because failure to obtain the visa blocks attendance (CTY: 'must request a nonimmigrant F-1 student visa' -- still not a nationality exclusion, but the practical bar is higher than Telluride's or PROMYS's disclaimers).

real_examples.quoted_language: The program is not able to assist with acquiring visas for international travel; international applicants must handle their own visa arrangements independently. This is stated as a logistics limitation, not an eligibility restriction -- both US and international students remain equally eligible to apply.

PROMYS students are not enrolled in college courses at Boston University, so participants come on a visitor's visa, not a student (F-1) visa. -- A factual documentation note, not a restriction; the same page affirmatively welcomes international applicants.

Non-U.S. citizens or non-U.S. permanent residents who are not already in the U.S. with an immigration status that allows study must request a nonimmigrant F-1 student visa to attend CTY's on-campus programs. -- A procedural requirement tied to attendance logistics, worded as a 'must obtain' rather than a nationality exclusion.

extraction_rules.when_to_mark_appears_open: Mark 'appears open' ONLY when (a) the page checked is clearly the program's own canonical eligibility/FAQ/rules page (not a marketing landing page, not a third-party aggregator/blog), AND (b) that page contains an explicit, affirmative statement that applicants of any nationality/country/citizenship are welcome (e.g. 'open to any country,' 'students worldwide,' 'no citizenship restriction') -- not merely the absence of a restriction elsewhere on the same page, AND (c) no other section of that same page introduces a narrower, unaddressed restriction (e.g. a grade-level or school-type rule) that would need its own separate classification. Record the exact quoted sentence and URL alongside the classification.
extraction_rules.when_to_mark_unknown_not_stated: This is the DEFAULT position and should be used whenever: the program's own eligibility/FAQ/rules page could not be located or fetched at all; a page was found but it describes some eligibility criteria (age, grade, subject) without affirmatively addressing citizenship/residency/international applicants either way (the Science Olympiad case); the only available source is a secondary/aggregator site (blog, 'how to apply' guide) rather than the org's own domain, even if that secondary source claims a specific answer; or the organizer's own materials indicate the answer is genuinely variable/non-public (RSI's annually-changing, unpublished 'participating countries' list). Do not upgrade 'unknown' to 'appears open' or 'restricted' based on inference from the organizer's type, country, or reputation.
extraction_rules.when_to_mark_restricted: Mark 'restricted' when the official page contains an explicit affirmative statement naming a citizenship requirement (e.g. 'must be a U.S. citizen'), a permanent-residency requirement, a sub-national domicile/residency requirement (e.g. 'must be a North Carolina resident'), or a current-school-enrollment-location requirement (e.g. 'available only to students who reside in the United States' / 'attending school in the U.S.'). When a program is restricted via a national-quota/nomination mechanism (EUCYS, UWC, ISEF) rather than a direct citizenship test, record it as restricted-via-national-mechanism with a note explaining the mechanism, rather than as a simple binary, since the practical answer for a given student depends on whether their country currently has an active national organiser/affiliate -- itself a fact requiring its own sourcing and periodic re-verification.
extraction_rules.general_non_fabrication_principle: Absence of a stated restriction is not evidence of an explicit opening, and organizer type/location is not a reliable proxy for restriction in either direction -- multiple US-university-hosted programs in this research (Yale YYGS, PROMYS, Diamond Challenge, Telluride TASS, John Locke) are explicitly open worldwide despite being US-based, while others (Simons, Davidson, MIT PRIMES, NASA) are tightly restricted despite superficially similar profiles. Every classification recorded must trace to a specific quoted sentence and URL; if no such quotable sentence exists, the correct output is 'unknown,' never a plausible-sounding guess, even when the guess would likely be correct (e.g. assuming a federal U.S. government program requires citizenship is usually right but must still be sourced before being stated as fact to a student).

data_model_gap_notes: No field captures 'current school enrollment location' as its own eligibility axis, distinct from citizenship and from domicile/residency -- needed for MIT PRIMES, QuestBridge's school-enrollment path, NC Governor's School's exchange-student exclusion, and Sutton Trust's state-school requirement.

No structured restriction_basis enum (citizenship | permanent_residency | domicile_residency | school_enrollment_location | national_quota_nomination | none_stated) exists to make citizenship_restrictions/residency_restrictions machine-queryable; today they are opaque free text, which is how ORYN's own Tisch NYU row ended up conflating an age rule, a housing rule, and a citizenship/visa-documentation rule into a single field.

No separate field exists for visa/documentation logistics notes (Telluride, PROMYS, CTY-style) that are explicitly NOT eligibility restrictions; today these have nowhere to go except residency_restrictions or citizenship_restrictions, which risks exactly the false impression this research was asked to avoid -- that a program mentioning visas is therefore closed to international students.

No mechanism exists to flag that an eligible-country list is organizer-determined and non-public/annually variable (RSI) rather than a fixed, citable fact -- a snapshot eligible_countries array would silently go stale or overstate certainty for this pattern.
eligible_countries as a flat array cannot represent sub-national restrictions (state/region-level, as in NC Governor's School) since it is country-granularity only.

eligible_countries as a flat array cannot represent national-quota/nomination-mediated programs (EUCYS, UWC, ISEF) without misleading simplification -- listing 'Turkey' as an eligible_country for EUCYS would be true only if Turkey currently has an active National Organiser sending a winning project that year, a fact the flat list cannot express.

No field distinguishes citizenship from permanent-residency status even though several programs explicitly treat them as equivalent ('citizens and/or permanent residents') -- this research did not find a real counter-example where the two are treated differently, but the schema currently has no way to represent that distinction if one is later found, since both would collapse into the same citizenship_restrictions text string.
unsafe_inferences: Assuming a program hosted at or run by a US university/organization defaults to 'US citizens/permanent residents only' -- contradicted by Yale YYGS, PROMYS, Diamond Challenge, Telluride TASS, and John Locke Institute, all explicitly open worldwide.

Treating the absence of eligibility language on a marketing/landing page as proof the program is open to all countries -- landing pages routinely omit eligibility detail that lives only on a dedicated FAQ/eligibility subpage.

Assuming 'the student currently attends school in the eligible country' satisfies a citizenship-status requirement, or vice versa -- Davidson Fellows/Simons/NASA require actual citizenship/PR status regardless of current school location; MIT PRIMES requires current US residency/school attendance regardless of citizenship. These are not substitutable.

Treating a country's appearance in a 'students from N countries have attended' promotional statistic as a guarantee that country is eligible in the current cycle -- RSI's participating-countries list is annually redetermined and not fixed.

Treating any mention of visa/F-1/immigration-status language as evidence of a nationality restriction -- Telluride, PROMYS, and CTY all mention visas while remaining open (or open-with-a-documentation-step) to international applicants.

Inferring 'restricted' purely because the word 'citizenship' or 'residency' never appears on a program's site -- some restrictions are phrased entirely in school-enrollment-location terms (MIT PRIMES never uses the word 'citizenship' at all).
safe_inferences: If the official eligibility/FAQ/rules page contains explicit language such as 'open to any country,' 'students worldwide,' or an equivalent affirmative statement, it is safe to record 'appears open,' quoting that language and its URL.

If the official page explicitly states a citizenship or permanent-residency requirement with no international alternative described, it is safe to record 'restricted -- citizenship/residency basis,' quoting that language.

If a program's stated application path requires nomination or qualification through a country-specific national committee, organiser, or affiliated fair, it is safe to record the mechanism explicitly (national-quota-mediated) rather than force it into a simple open/restricted binary, since the real-world answer depends on a fact (does an active organiser exist for this student's country this cycle) that itself needs its own verification and refresh cycle.

If a program's own materials draw an explicit line between where a student currently attends school/resides and their citizenship (as QuestBridge and DAAD RISE both do, each offering two distinct qualifying paths), it is safe to preserve both facts as separate structured data points rather than merging them, since they can and do produce different eligibility outcomes for the same individual student.
unresolved_questions: How should ORYN represent eligible-country lists that are organizer-determined and non-public/annually variable (RSI) -- a boolean 'list_is_non_public_and_variable' flag plus a mandatory re-verification cadence, or something else?

Should national-quota/nomination-mediated programs (EUCYS, UWC, ISEF) get their own eligibility_type value, or is that too complex for a student-facing product that mainly needs a fast yes/no/unclear read -- i.e., is there a tradeoff between taxonomic accuracy and UI simplicity that needs a product decision, not just a data-model one?

This research did not find a real example of a program that accepts citizenship but explicitly excludes permanent residents (or vice versa) -- do such programs exist in ORYN's actual 352-row dataset, and if so, does the schema need a citizenship/permanent-residency split, or is 'citizens and/or permanent residents' effectively always treated as one bucket in practice?

Where should visa/documentation logistics notes (Telluride/PROMYS/CTY-style) live in the schema -- a new dedicated field, or deliberately left out of ORYN's structured data entirely and only surfaced via the source link, given they are informational rather than eligibility-determining?

How should ORYN handle sub-national (state/region-level) residency restrictions like NC Governor's School within a country-granularity eligible_countries field -- is this common enough across the 352-row dataset to justify a geographic_scope (country vs. region/state) field, or rare enough to leave as free text?

What confidence tier, if any, should apply to eligibility facts sourced only via a search-engine paraphrase of an official page that itself could not be directly fetched (the RSI case in this research) -- should ORYN require a second, independent confirmation before treating such a fact as anything above 'low confidence'?

stale_vs_current_signals: CURRENT signal: the page states an explicit future or in-progress deadline with a specific date/time and no closure language (e.g. Regeneron STS: 'now open through 8PM ET on Thursday, November 5, 2026').

STALE signal: the page states 'Applications are now closed' / 'applications closed on [past date]' without being updated to the next cycle -- this is the single clearest lexical marker found across every category researched.

STALE signal (subtler, and the most dangerous for ORYN): a page shows a specific PAST calendar year in its title, dates, or 'Apply by [date]' language with no closure statement at all -- e.g. a program page that still displays 'RSI 2024' or 'Summer 2023 program dates' with no update; several secondary/aggregator sources returned by search were themselves stale in exactly this way (guide articles referencing 2024/2025 cycles), which is a caution for any pipeline that scrapes aggregator content rather than official pages.

CURRENT/transitional signal: pages that explicitly name BOTH the just-closed cycle and the next cycle together ('Applications for 2026 have closed. Please check back in October for 2027 program details.') are unambiguous and safest to parse -- the presence of a forward-pointing 'next cycle' year is the strongest positive signal that the page is being actively maintained, versus a page that only shows a past year with no forward pointer.

AMBIGUOUS case worth flagging: cycle-year numbering conventions are inconsistent across programs -- some label by the program/cohort year (Regeneron 'STS 2027' for an application closing Nov 2026), others by application-opening academic year (Coca-Cola 'graduating high school during the 2026-2027 academic year'), and others by literal calendar program dates (MD Anderson 'June 1 - August 7, 2026'). A `current_cycle_label` field cannot assume a single numbering convention; it must be parsed per-program rather than pattern-matched against one fixed 'YYYY' regex.

Rolling-deadline programs (NASA OSTEM, some CTY tracks) do not have a single 'closed/open' binary at all -- they cycle through several session windows per year, so a 'stale' determination for these requires checking whether the MOST RECENT of several session dates has passed, not just whether any deadline text is present.

unsafe_inferences: Do not assume every program in a category shares the same prerequisite pattern -- within 'research' alone, Simons explicitly disclaims a prior-research requirement while MIT PRIMES explicitly expects 'a very advanced background' and named prior programs; category-level defaults will misclassify specific programs.

Do not infer a numeric GPA threshold when a program uses qualitative language ('strong academic record,' 'rigorous coursework') -- most programs researched (Simons, PRIMES, HIP-SAT, SIMR) deliberately avoid a hard GPA number even when GPA clearly matters to selection; inventing a number from vague language would violate ORYN's no-false-precision principle just as much as inventing an admissions probability would.

Do not treat 'school sponsorship required' as universal for competitions -- Science Olympiad and National Science Bowl require it (school-designated regional/single-school team), but Regeneron STS is explicitly individual research with no school-team structure, and Diamond Challenge requires only a generic 'adult advisor' who need not be from the student's school.

Do not assume a single 'YYYY' regex safely extracts the current cycle year -- the same literal year number can refer to different things across programs (cohort year vs. academic year vs. deadline year vs. program-start year), and a naive extraction risks silently mislabeling a closed cycle as current or vice versa.

Do not assume 'applications closed' automatically means the row should be hidden/deprioritized without checking whether the page also names the next cycle -- some 'closed' pages (Seattle Children's, MD Anderson) are more current/trustworthy signals of an actively maintained program than a page with a stale, unlabeled deadline from a prior year and no closure statement at all.

Do not use secondary/aggregator 'guide' sites (Pioneer Academics, AdmissionSight, CollegeEssayGuy, Immerse Education, etc.) as the sole source for any single fact -- several of these sites' own indexed pages referenced stale years (2024/2025) even while writing about 'current' cycles, showing that aggregators themselves lag official sources and should only be used for discovery, exactly as ORYN's stated source standard specifies.

Do not assume rolling-admission programs have no risk of staleness -- NASA OSTEM and CTY's session-based rolling deadlines still have real per-session close dates that pass; 'rolling' is not synonymous with 'always open.'
safe_inferences: A page containing both a past-tense closure statement ('applications closed on [date]') AND a named next-cycle year or a 'check back in [month]' pointer is a strong CURRENT/well-maintained signal, even though the immediate application itself is closed -- ORYN should distinguish 'closed-but-freshly-maintained' from 'stale-and-abandoned' rather than collapsing both into one 'closed' state.

Competitions that are team-based and multi-round (robotics, science bowl, entrepreneurship challenges) reliably separate a registration/entry deadline from the event date(s) -- this justifies ORYN modeling `deadline` as potentially plural/staged for competition-category rows rather than a single field, at least for well-known team competitions.

Scholarships reliably run one deadline per applicant-track per year tied to graduating class or academic year, which supports a simpler single `deadline` + `current_cycle_label` (formatted as an academic-year span, e.g. '2026-2027') model for that category specifically.

Research programs reliably show a single winter/spring deadline for a summer cohort -- this is consistent enough across RSI, Simons, MITES, and SIMR that a 'one annual deadline, ~4-6 months before program start' default is a reasonable prior for this category, while still requiring per-program verification before display.

When a program explicitly disclaims a prerequisite ('prior research experience is not a prerequisite,' 'PROMYS does not require prior calculus'), that disclaimer is itself useful structured data for ORYN's advisor -- it tells a student that a commonly assumed barrier does not actually apply, which is exactly the kind of fact-vs-assumption distinction the advisor is supposed to surface.

GPA numbers, when actually stated, tend to cluster in two clear bands across the programs found: ~3.0 as a baseline eligibility floor (Coca-Cola Scholars, general OSTEM) and ~3.3 as a 'strong academic standing' floor (Gates Scholarship) -- useful as a rough calibration reference, not as a rule to impute onto programs that don't state a number.
unresolved_questions: Could not independently verify verbatim text from several official pages that blocked automated fetching (403 responses) -- notably cee.org (RSI), stonybrook.edu (Simons), cty.jhu.edu (CTY), horatioalger.org, med.stanford.edu, drew.edu (NJ Governor's School), chemistry.berkeley.edu (SYIP). For these, the quoted language in this file is drawn from search-engine-rendered excerpts of the official pages (in most cases) rather than a direct live fetch, and should be re-verified by a human or a differently-configured fetcher before being treated as fully authoritative by ORYN.

Could not find an official page that unambiguously states an internship-specific (not general OSTEM/college-level) GPA requirement for a high-school-eligible NASA internship track -- the 3.0 GPA figure is documented on NASA's general OSTEM page, which explicitly frames its eligibility text around college students; whether the identical 3.0 threshold applies to the youngest eligible (16+, high-school) applicants was not independently confirmed on an HS-specific page.

Could not find a real, currently-active program with an explicit, hard-stated coursework prerequisite in the strict sense the task asked about (e.g. 'must have completed AP Chemistry or equivalent' as a literal named-course gate). Every program found that touches coursework (SIMR, HIP-SAT, MITES, PRIMES, RSI) uses qualitative/preference language ('strong preparation,' 'rigorous coursework,' 'advanced background') rather than naming a specific required course by name. This is itself a finding worth surfacing to ORYN: named-course prerequisites appear to be rare-to-nonexistent among elite/selective US programs researched, which typically prefer to gate on demonstrated ability (test scores, GPA, portfolio, recommendation) rather than a specific transcript line item -- but this could not be verified in more heavily coursework-gated domains ORYN's database likely also contains (e.g. European program-specific subject prerequisites, medical/health-track programs, or engineering programs with named-course gates like 'completed Algebra II'), which fell outside the scope of what was searched.

Could not access an official Governor's School (NJ or Kentucky) page directly (fetches returned only navigation, not body content) to verify whether these state-run academic programs state any coursework prerequisite beyond the junior-year/nomination requirement found via search summaries -- flagged as an open gap rather than resolved.

The scope of 'real, currently active programs' researched here skews heavily toward well-known, elite/selective US-based programs (RSI, PRIMES, Simons, Regeneron STS, QuestBridge, Gates Scholarship, etc.) because these dominate search results and have well-maintained official pages. ORYN's actual database is 67% summer_program and heavily populated with less prominent programs; the patterns documented here (soft qualitative prerequisites, priority/regular deadline tiers, explicit stale/current cycle language) may be less reliably present -- or stated in less standardized language -- on the pages of smaller or less resourced programs that were not sampled in this research pass.

Volunteering and fellowship categories (1 and 2 rows respectively in ORYN's live data) were not researched at all per the task's explicit scope (5 major categories only); no claims should be inferred about those categories from this file.
